# Releasing

How a version of `forge` is cut, and the two things about this repository that
make it more than `git tag`.

Nothing is released yet. What follows is the process the first tag establishes,
written down before it is needed rather than after somebody has had to guess.

## What a version means

Three of them, and they can disagree. Every generated file records all three in
its header, and each disagreement means something different:

```
// Code generated by forge. DO NOT EDIT.
//
// forge (devel)
// markers github.com/okian/forge (devel)
// go go1.27.1
// inputs e9c6d570e167a992
```

- **forge** is the version of the binary that wrote the file. It says which
  generator produced it.
- **markers** is the module a spec file imports, and its version. It says which
  declarations the binary can resolve — a spec naming a marker the binary has
  never heard of is the failure this line explains.
- **go** is the toolchain that formatted the output, which is the one of the
  three that changes what the bytes are.
- **inputs** is a digest over the declaration, its options, the subject it
  reaches, and all three versions above. `forge check` compares it, which is how
  a stale file is found without regenerating one.

`(devel)` is what `go run` produces, and what `go build -buildvcs=false`
produces — there is no version to record, and saying so beats inventing one. A
plain `go build` is different: it stamps a pseudo-version derived from the
checkout, `v0.0.0-20260902162532-3b048d461559+dirty`, which moves on every
commit.
That is why the regeneration targets in the Makefile pass `-buildvcs=false`: a
committed file whose header moved because somebody rebuilt is a file in every
review, saying nothing in any of them.

The **markers** line is a constant path with a looked-up version, not the
running binary's module — because a binary somebody linked a layer into has a
module of its own, and the markers a spec file names are still forge's. A header
recording the running module would claim a file was written against markers that
module does not declare, and `check` compares that line: every file such a
binary wrote would look like the work of different tooling.

## Cutting a release

1. **Move `Unreleased` into a version.** In
   [`CHANGELOG.md`](../CHANGELOG.md), rename the heading to
   `## vX.Y.Z — YYYY-MM-DD` and open a fresh `## Unreleased` above it. The shape
   is checked by a test, so a heading that does not read as a version fails the
   build rather than the release.

2. **Run `make ci`, not `make check`.** `make check` is the fast subset:
   `fmt-check vet lint cover` over both modules, plus `size` over this one. It
   leaves out the race detector, both benchmark suites, the fuzz targets,
   `tidy-check` and `govulncheck`, and cutting a tag is the one moment their
   cost is obviously worth paying. `make ci` runs the lot, which is every gate
   the pipeline runs. `tidy-check` is the gate behind the `make tidy` that
   step 2 of the publishing order below calls for.

3. **Regenerate the committed output and commit any diff.** `make example`,
   `make layers-example` and `make diagnostics`. A release whose examples were
   written by an older binary ships documentation that disagrees with the tool.

4. **Tag the module.** `git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`. That is the
   whole of it for `github.com/okian/forge`, and the module proxy picks it up on
   the first fetch.

5. **Tag `x/csv` separately** — see below. A release that tags only the root
   leaves it unfetchable at any version. `benchmarks/validator` is a module for
   the go command's benefit and nobody fetches it, so it takes no tag.

Versions follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). What the promise
covers is [`plugin`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/okian/forge/plugin), the
`forge` command's flags and output, and the shape of what is generated: a
declaration that generated a working package under `vX.Y` generates a working
package under `vX.Y+1`. What it does not cover is the exact bytes. A better
comment or a tighter loop in what forge emits is a *patch* release and still
rewrites every committed file in every checkout, which is why it is called out
in the changelog whether or not the API moved.

`driver` is covered too, and has to be: `driver.Builtins`, `driver.Main` and
`driver.Run` are what every out-of-tree layer binary's `main` compiles against,
so a signature there breaks all of them at once. So are the marker types in the
root `forge` package, which are what every spec file names.

`internal/` is not covered and never will be. Everything in it that anybody
outside may reach is reached through `plugin` or `driver`, and those two are
where the promise is made.

## The nested modules

Two directories are modules of their own, which the go command reads as not part
of the module above them:

| Directory              | Module path                             | Why it is separate                                    |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `x/csv`                | `github.com/okian/forge/x/csv`          | so it cannot reach past the published `plugin` surface |
| `benchmarks/validator` | `github.com/okian/forge/benchmarks/validator` | so the module everybody builds keeps its one direct dependency |

**A nested module is tagged with its directory as the prefix.** `x/csv` at
version 1.0.0 is the tag `x/csv/v1.0.0`, not `v1.0.0` — the go command derives
one from the other, and there is no way to fetch a subdirectory module from a
bare version tag. `benchmarks/validator` is never fetched by anybody and needs
no tag at all.

**And its requirement has to name a version that exists.** `x/csv/go.mod`
currently carries

```
require github.com/okian/forge v0.0.0

replace github.com/okian/forge => ../..
```

which is what makes local development work and what makes the module
unfetchable. A consumer's own module ignores a dependency's `replace`
directives, so what a consumer sees is a requirement on `v0.0.0`:

```
go: downloading github.com/okian/forge v0.0.0
go: github.com/okian/forge/x/csv imports
	github.com/okian/forge/plugin: reading github.com/okian/forge/go.mod
	at revision v0.0.0: unknown revision v0.0.0
```

That is a direct fetch. Through the default proxy the wording is a 404 on the
module zip instead, which means the same thing.

So publishing `x/csv` is four steps, in this order:

1. Tag the root module first, so there is a version to require.
2. In `x/csv/go.mod`, require that version and delete the `replace`. Then run
   `make tidy` — not `tidy-check`, which only reports — so that `x/csv/go.sum`
   gains the root module's hashes. It has none today, because a directory
   replacement produces no hash to record. A consumer is unaffected either way,
   since the go command verifies against the main module's `go.sum` and never
   reads a dependency's; what breaks without them is this module's own build,
   and `tidy-check` going red is how you find out.
3. Commit that. A tag names a commit, and this is the commit whose `go.mod` a
   consumer will read.
4. Tag `x/csv/vX.Y.Z` on it.

Its version is its own. The prefix ties the tag to the directory and nothing
ties the number to the root module's, which is half the point of a nested
module: a layer can reach v2 over a forge that is still on v1.

Reaching v2 costs one thing more. A module at v2 or above carries the major in
its path, so it becomes `github.com/okian/forge/x/csv/v2` — a `go.mod` edit and
an import path every consumer rewrites — while the tag stays `x/csv/v2.0.0`,
since the prefix is the directory and the directory has not moved.

Local development after that runs through a `go.work` rather than a replace,
which is the tool for exactly this: the requirement in `go.mod` stays the one a
consumer would resolve, and the workspace is what points a local build at the
tree instead.

`go.work` is not committed, and not because of what it holds — `go work init .
./x/csv` writes relative paths and would work in anybody's checkout. It is not
committed because a committed workspace applies to everybody who clones, which
puts every build on the tree rather than on the published requirement. A
`go.mod` naming a version nobody can resolve would then keep working here and
fail for the first person outside, which is the exact failure this section is
about.

Until step 1 has happened, `x/csv` is a worked example that builds in this
checkout and cannot be fetched. That is a deliberate state and not an oversight
— there is nothing to require yet — but it is the reason the README describes it
as something to read rather than something to `go get`.

## What is not automated, and why

There is no release workflow. Tagging is one command and a release is a
judgement about whether the surface moved, which is not a judgement to hand to a
runner — and a workflow that tags on a push is one that tags a mistake as
readily as a release.

What CI does gate is everything a release depends on: both modules'
formatting, vet in both build configurations, the linter's budgets, the coverage
floor, the race detector, the benchmarks against their budgets, the codec fuzz
targets, cross-compilation for five platforms, tidiness, and reachable
vulnerabilities. A green `ci` job is the precondition; the tag is the decision.
